description_full: Empire State Realty Trust, Inc. is a NYC-focused REIT that owns and operates a portfolio of well-leased, top of tier, modernized, amenitized, and well-located office, retail, and multifamily assets. The Company is a recognized leader in energy efficiency and indoor environmental quality. As of June 30, 2026, ESRT's portfolio is comprised of approximately 7.5 million rentable square feet of office space, 0.8 million rentable square feet of retail space and 743 residential units. Empire State Realty Trust, Inc. was established on July 29, 2011, and was incorporated in 2011 in Maryland and is based in New York.
ceo_bio: Mr. Anthony E. Malkin | Chairman & CEO | Age 63 | Compensation: $3.2M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 642 people. Revenue per employee of $1.2M ranks in the below the sector median among Real Estate peers, improving at 12%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $79K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $39K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 3× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10).
financial_summary: Empire State Realty Trust, Inc. is a small-cap real estate business with a $1.6B market cap on $768M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 20% against a 10% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $51M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.74× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 1.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.
Shareholder yield is only 2.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 7.7% of the shares.

sect: Its 18% operating margin trails the Real Estate median (23%) by 5pp, so it is a below-average operator in its field.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.89x).
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 145 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 38% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 10% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 30% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 0.96, it moves roughly with the market.
About $18.4M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.9x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 58% in the 2020 crash and 36% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $3.65 (margin of safety -45%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 22%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $2.32 to $6.16 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Real Estate peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 9.7 vs 16.3, richer on P/E 88.5 vs 23.6 and P/FCF 31.7 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 46% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $5.20 on average, 2% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 20% clears the cost of capital of 9.6% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.34).
It converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow, or 3% after stock compensation.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 7%.
ROE of 4% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (4.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 3.3% of revenue on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 0.62 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.9% over 3 years, 4.7% over 5 years and 1.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 57%).
At current returns, reinvesting 3% of profits supports about 0.6% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -8.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 6.4% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 25.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 7.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Shareholder yield is a modest 2.0% (0.5% in buybacks and 2.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.8% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 700% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 642 employees, each generates about $1.2M of revenue, 0.5x the Real Estate median, and productivity has risen 11.6% a year.
That works out to $79K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.2M (3x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
